quotedTweet.text:
Crude refining margin 101

The price of crude delivered to refinery = Benchmark + FOB premium + freight cost

Benchmark can be ICE Brent, Dated Brent, Nymex WTI or Dubai.

FOB premium is a factor of supply and demand, quality of crude and logistics. If that crude is red hot in demand, FOB goes up. FOB premium is also known as cash diff/differential.

Freight cost has its own supply and demand angle. Right now VLCCs are in short supply due to highly inefficient logistics caused by the war, hence the crazy valuations there.

Crude margins is then the value of the crude minus the delivered price of crude. The value of the crude is also known as gross product worth (GPW). You multiply product cracks with the yields obtained from the crude.

Each refinery values the crude differently due to unique refining configurations. They run Linear Programming (LPs) to obtain these valuations.

In the current climate, refining margin must be ≥0 since refining is short. If it goes below 0, then something in the equation needs to adjust. I.e. either FOB  premium or freight goes down, or product cracks rise. 

In Sparta, we model all of the above and align 90 crudes to the same delivery window for 8 refining destinations with 3 different refining configurations per region.

Hope this explains the basics of crude refining economics.

The latest COT report on #commodities, covering the week to 20 October, showed net selling extending into a sixth consecutive week, during which the BCOM Index has fallen by 8%.

Once again, the bulk of the selling was concentrated in natural gas and metals, led by gold and, not least, copper. Grains also continued to attract selling, with the combined net long tumbling by 42% over the past four weeks after reaching an unsustainable record above 1 million contracts last month.

Across crude oil and refined products, demand was muted during a week of mixed price performance, with crude rallying while fuel products eased. The Brent net long 242k contracts was in line with the average seen during the past two months, and well below the 430k long recorded at the start of the Middle East disruption. 

In softs, all four contracts attracted net buying, led by coffee and sugar, with the latter's speculative net long reaching a fresh five-year high.

LME copper stocks in US climb to 12-year high.
Copper inventories in London Metal Exchange warehouses in the US have swelled to their highest in 12-1/2 years as metal continues to accumulate in the country ahead of possible import tariffs from the start of next year. Stocks in US LME warehouses, mostly in New Orleans and Baltimore — now stand at 169,475 metric tons, the most since April 2014. They account for around 62% of all copper inventory on the exchange, the highest percentage since March 2019. (Reuters)

A clarification on US-held copper stocks: While COMEX inventories are generally duty-paid and inside the US tariff wall, copper held in bonded LME warehouses is not. So why the buildup?

The attraction is flexibility. Traders can store copper close to US consumers, ready for customs clearance if market conditions warrant, while retaining the option to re-export without incurring US import duties. This has become particularly attractive amid uncertainty over future tariffs and shifts in the COMEX–LME arbitrage.

In short, US-based LME warehouses offer proximity to the US market without immediately committing to US import duties, although any future tariff would generally apply when the metal enters domestic circulation.

#Copper inventories monitored by the three major futures exchanges have risen for a fourth consecutive week to 1.05 million tonnes, with a 19.6 kt drop in Shanghai to a 2-1/2 year low being offset by a 6.8 kt increase on COMEX and a 47.5 kt jump at LME, however with the bulk of that going into US based warehouses. As highlighted previously, the build remains heavily concentrated in the US, where combined COMEX and LME warehouse stocks have reached 893,000 tonnes, or 85% of the global exchange-monitored total. This remarkable concentration reflects months of tariff-driven stockpiling, leaving inventories outside the US relatively tight despite the overall increase. 

Against this backdrop, traders are likely to intensify their focus on Washington and its pending decision on whether to impose tariffs on refined copper imports, potentially starting in January 2027. A decision against tariffs could trigger an unwinding of the stockpiling trade, putting pressure on U.S. versus ROW spreads and potentially releasing US-held metal back into the global market. Such a development could weigh on prices, although the speed and scale of any physical outflows would depend on the relative price incentives and costs of moving the metal.
